'''Tie''': {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No votes}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Lawton Chiles]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Lawton Chiles]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsFL}} The '''1994 Florida gubernatorial election''' was held on November 8, 1994. Democratic incumbent [[Lawton Chiles]] was narrowly re-elected to a second term over Republican former [[Florida Department of Commerce|Florida commerce secretary]] [[Jeb Bush]]. This race was the second-closest gubernatorial election in Florida history, after the [[1876 Florida gubernatorial election|1876 election]], due to the [[Republican Revolution|strong Republican wave of 1994]]. As of {{CURRENTYEAR}}, this is the last time a Democrat was elected governor of Florida. Primary elections were held on September 8. Chiles dispatched a challenge from populist activist [[Jack Gargan (politician)|Jack Gargan]] to win the Democratic nomination. Bush won a plurality of the Republican primary vote, with particular strength in [[Miami-Dade County, Florida|Dade County]]. Although [[Secretary of State of Florida|Florida secretary of state]] [[James C. Smith (politician)|James C. Smith]] finished second and was entitled to challenge Bush in a runoff election, he declined and Bush was certified as the Republican nominee. == Background == Lawton Chiles was eligible to run for a second four-year term under the [[Constitution of Florida]]. In late 1991, Chiles's [[Disapproval voting|disapproval rating]] rose significantly after he cut funds for education in his first budget. Around 75 percent of Floridians gave him a fair or poor performance rating.{{cite book|author=John Dos Passos Coggin|title=Walkin' Lawton|publisher=The Florida Historical Society Press|location=Cocoa, Florida|date=November 20, 2012|pages=323–324, 386|isbn=978-1886104587}} The following year, Chiles's approval rating fell to only 22 percent after the perceptions that the state response to [[Hurricane Andrew]] was inadequate.{{cite news|url=http://www.tampabay.com/news/politics/national/poll-rick-scott-one-of-the-nations-least-popular-governors/1171680|title=Poll: Rick Scott one of the nation's least popular governors|author=Marc Caputo|date=May 25, 2011|newspaper=[[Tampa Bay Times]]|access-date=October 3, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170905233809/http://www.tampabay.com/news/politics/national/poll-rick-scott-one-of-the-nations-least-popular-governors/1171680|archive-date=2017-09-05|url-status=dead}} His disapproval rating remained as high as 71 percent into 1993. C." Reed, former trucking and moving industry worker (Independent) ===Campaign=== Bush ran as a political conservative and tried to paint Chiles as beholden to liberal interests. At one point, when asked what he would do for [[African American]]s, Bush responded, "It's time to strive for a society where there's [[Equal opportunity|equality of opportunity]], not [[Equality of outcome|equality of results]]. So I'm going to answer your question by saying: probably nothing."{{cite book|author1=Joel Aberbach |author2=Gillian Peele |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QE7U4-Ion7kC&pg=PA189|title=Crisis of Conservatism?: The Republican Party, the Conservative Movement, and American Politics After Bush|page=189|publisher=Oxford University Press|date=2011|location=New York|isbn=9780199831364 }} The final weeks of the campaign was described as "one of the nastiest in Florida political history."{{cite news|url=http://nl.newsbank.com/nl-search/we/Archives?p_product=AT&p_theme=at&p_action=search&p_maxdocs=200&p_field_label-0=Author&p_field_label-1=title&p_bool_label-1=AND&s_dispstring=mudslinging%20campaign%20tarnishes%20AND%20date(11/12/1994%20to%2011/13/1994)&p_field_date-0=YMD_date&p_params_date-0=date:B,E&p_text_date-0=11/12/1994%20to%2011/13/1994)&p_field_advanced-0=&p_text_advanced-0=(mudslinging%20campaign%20tarnishes)&xcal_numdocs=40&p_perpage=20&p_sort=_rank_:D&xcal_ranksort=4&xcal_useweights=yes|title=Mudslinging campaign tarnishes Chiles' easy-going image|author=Mike Williams|date=November 13, 1994|publisher=[[The Atlanta Journal-Constitution]]|pages=4|access-date=October 3, 2015|location=Tallahassee, Florida}} On the day before the election, the Chiles campaign called about 70,000 Floridians in a [[get out the vote]] effort. Their calls alleged that Bush was a "tax cheat" and that his running mate [[Tom Feeney]] planned to destroy Social Security, and the callers falsely attributed these claims to "tax fairness" and senior citizen advocacy organizations. Chiles denied authorizing the phone calls but still later apologized when the media discovered top officials in his campaign had authorized them. Bush and Chiles stood behind two lecterns decorated with [[Mickey Mouse]] ears.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/10/19/us/1994-campaign-florida-governor-jeb-bush-debate-exchanging-taunts-claims.html|title=The 1994 Campaign: Florida; Governor and Jeb Bush Debate, Exchanging Taunts and Claims of Distorting Truth|date=October 19, 1994|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=October 3, 2015|location=Orlando, Florida}} On November 1, another debate between Bush and Chiles was conducted by the [[League of Women Voters of Florida]] at [[Straz Center for the Performing Arts|Tampa Performing Arts Center]]. Early in the debate, Chiles again criticized Bush's ad about the death penalty, stating that Bush had outdone his father's ad about [[Willie Horton]] and saying "You knew [the ad] was false. You admitted it was false. And I am ashamed that you would use the loss of a mother in an ad like this." Later, during a discussion about school vouchers, Chiles quipped "My mama told me, 'sticks and stones will break my bones,' but names will never hurt me. But let me tell you one other thing about the old liberal. The old He-Coon walks just before the light of day." This referenced Chiles' [[Florida cracker]] roots, and served as a deliberate contrast with the more urbane Bush. === Campaign finance === Throughout the campaign, Bush raised approximately $7 million, more than half of which came from fundraisers featuring his parents and out-of-state fundraisers sponsored by his [[Bush family|family]] and friends. On each of [[Barbara Bush|Barbara]] and George H. W. Bush's visits to Florida, they raked in about $1 million for the campaign.{{cite book|author=Robert E. Crew Jr.|title=Jeb Bush: Aggressive Conservatism in Florida|publisher=University Press of America|location=Lanham, Maryland|date=December 2, 2009|page=7|isbn=9780761849841|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0m-gMZ6E9ooC|access-date=October 3, 2015}} Chiles limited contributions to $100 per person and raised $6.23 million, which included $2 million in public money. === Results === Chiles prevailed against Bush by about 1.52 percent of the vote. Amid the [[Republican Revolution]] of 1994, Chiles was one of two Democratic governors to win close races to hold their seat that night, along with [[Zell Miller]] of neighboring [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]]. However, Republicans gained control of the [[Florida Senate]] for the first time in over a century, [[United States Senate|U.S. senator]] [[Connie Mack III]] was reelected to a second term in a landslide, and Republicans won races for Secretary of State, Comptroller, and Commissioner of Education. A statewide ballot initiative to legalize [[casino]] [[gambling]] was defeated with only 38 percent of the vote.{{cite news|title=$16 million ad blitz fails to sway voters (Part 1)|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/6545845//|first=John|last=Fernandez|newspaper=The Palm Beach Post|page=1|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=November 9, 1994|access-date=September 7, 2016}}{{Open access}}{{cite news|title=Pro-casino group pledges return in '96 (Part 2)|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/6545880//|first=John|last=Fernandez|newspaper=The Palm Beach Post|page=9|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=November 9, 1994|access-date=September 7, 2016}}{{Open access}} In comparison with the 1990 election, Chiles performed significantly worse in [[North Florida|North]] and [[Central Florida]].{{Election box begin | title=Florida gubernatorial election, 1994{{cite web |url=https://doe.dos.state.fl.us/elections/resultsarchive/Index.asp?ElectionDate%3D11%2F8%2F1994%26DATAMODE%3D |title=Florida Department of State - Chiles also carried the other two major urban [[South Florida]] counties, [[Broward County, Florida|Broward]] and [[Palm Beach County, Florida|Palm Beach]]. Although he lost several counties in the [[Florida Panhandle|Panhandle]] which he had won in 1990, including his native [[Polk County, Florida|Polk County]], Chiles' largest margin of victory was in [[Gadsden County, Florida|Gadsden County]], the only plurality [[African Americans|African American]] county in Florida. style="text-align:center;"|''0'' | style="text-align:center;"|6,208 |} ==Aftermath== === Phonegate === After the election, the controversial phone calls were labeled "Phonegate." Bill Cotterell of the ''[[Tallahassee Democrat]]'' believed that the phone calls did not affect the result of the election, arguing, "I'm quite sure you know, at least half of them just hung up, never even listened to the message. And those who did probably said, well, that's ridiculous, the governor of Florida ... or the lieutenant governor of Florida can't repeal Social Security." ''[[Miami Herald]]'' writer Mark Silva also argued that the phone calls did not impact the outcome of the election, saying, "[the] campaign was won before that happened. The idea that that somehow tipped the election was a canard, it wasn't true." In November 1995, Bush campaign manager [[Mac Stipanovich]] claimed, "[I]t's quite possible the Chiles campaign stole the election by fraud". Bush himself refused to speculate on the impact of the phone calls. In December 1995, Chiles became the first modern Florida governor to testify under oath before a [[Florida Legislature|state legislative]] committee, the [[Florida Senate|Senate]] Committee on Executive Business, Ethics, and Elections. Chiles testified that he had no knowledge of the calls and apologized to any Floridians who may have been misled. Eventually, the opposition to Chiles was reduced to state senator [[Charlie Crist]]. Later, the Republican legislature passed a law banning false attributions for get out the vote calls, which Chiles signed. Chiles remained governor until suffering a fatal heart attack on December 12, 1998, less than a month before his second term expired. === Impact on Bush's presidential ambitions === Bush had originally planned on running for [[2000 United States presidential election|president of the United States in 2000]]. However, because he lost this election while his brother, [[George W. Bush]], was elected [[governor of Texas]] on the [[1994 Texas gubernatorial election|same night]], George ran for president in 2000.{{cite news|url=http://www.msnbc.com/hardball/the-he-coon-who-changed-history|title=The He-Coon who changed Jeb Bush's political career|author=Steve Kornacki|author-link=Steve Kornacki|date=April 25, 2014|newspaper=[[MSNBC]]|access-date=October 2, 2015}} Although Jeb Bush was elected governor [[1998 Florida gubernatorial election|in 1998]] and easily reelected [[2002 Florida gubernatorial election|in 2002]],{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2002/11/07/us/the-2002-elections-florida-bush-looks-to-2nd-term-as-analysts-point-to-2004.html|title=The 2002 Elections: Florida; Bush Looks to 2nd Term As Analysts Point to 2004|author=Dana Canedy|date=November 7, 2002|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=October 2, 2015|location=Miami, Florida}} his only campaign for president resulted in his defeat in the [[2016 Republican Party presidential primaries|2016 primaries]] by [[Donald Trump]]. == References == {{Reflist}} {{United States elections, 1994}} {{FlGovElections}} [[Category:Florida gubernatorial elections|1994]] [[Category:1994 United States gubernatorial elections|Florida]] [[Category:1994 elections in Florida|Gubernatorial]] [[Category:Jeb Bush]]
